Trump Proposes AI Force and New Name for AI, While Tech Leaders Warn of Risks

President Donald Trump has proposed creating an "AI Force" modeled on the Space Force and plans to appoint an AI czar, according to multiple outlets. He also suggested alternative names for artificial intelligence, including "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," and "Supreme Intelligence," calling the current term "inaccurate" and "very ineloquent." Trump has consistently defended the AI industry, claiming that the only control needed is a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT," which he asserts the U.S. has in abundance.

The AI industry has faced growing concerns from major companies and experts, who have warned of the technology's potential risks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Elon Musk have all called for slowing AI development to ensure safety measures keep pace with advancements. Some lawmakers have also expressed concerns, with Republican senators like Josh Hawley and Jon Husted pushing for legislation to address data security and infrastructure costs related to AI.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that the Defense Production Act (DPA) could be used to regulate AI if it poses a national security threat, and that Congress has extended most of the DPA's authorities through December 2026. This is not mentioned in the other accounts. The Hill notes that Trump posted a poll asking followers to vote on new names for AI, while Straight Arrow News adds that Trump also asked the public to weigh in on a new name for AI, suggesting "Superior Intelligence," "Extreme Intelligence," or "Supreme Intelligence." The Hill and Axios both mention Trump's proposal for an AI czar, but only Axios provides details about the lack of specifics on the role's responsibilities or budget.

Sources Slate · FOX News · Axios · BBC · The Hill · Straight Arrow News

Trump returns to White House as State Department issues security alerts for Middle East

President Trump cut his weekend trip to Camp David short a day early, returning to Washington, D.C., on Saturday evening. The White House pool report noted his arrival at the Ellipse just before 8 p.m. The return followed a new security alert issued by the State Department, which warned Americans in the Middle East to “exercise heightened vigilance” and prepare for potential travel disruptions due to attacks from the Iranian-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia confirmed that the Houthis attempted to attack its capital with a ballistic missile, according to The Associated Press. The Houthi military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, stated the group used “a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles” and drones to target Riyadh and Aramco facilities in Yanbu. This marks the first time the Houthis have targeted Riyadh since the conflict with Saudi Arabia intensified.

The White House revised Trump’s schedule to bring him back Saturday evening, with a press gathering set for 7 p.m. ET. The State Department issued identical warnings from U.S. diplomatic posts in Saudi Arabia and Jerusalem, advising travelers to sign up for the government’s traveler enrollment program and to remain cautious. The U.S. Mission in Iraq also issued a security alert, warning of hostilities against Saudi Arabia and advising travelers to brace for flight cancellations and airspace shutdowns.

Where the accounts differ

The Hill and The Daily Caller both report that Saudi Arabia confirmed the Houthis attempted to attack Riyadh with a ballistic missile, but The Daily Caller adds that the strike was intercepted and that some residents reported hearing a blast and seeing smoke near the airport. The Hill does not mention the interception or the smoke. The Washington Examiner describes smoke plumes over Riyadh’s airport and air raid alerts, but does not mention the missile attack. The Christian Science Monitor and NPR do not mention Trump’s return to Washington or the White House’s security alerts. Al Jazeera reports that Saudi authorities issued air raid alerts and that at least one explosion was heard in Riyadh, with smoke seen near the airport, but does not mention the missile attack.

Sources The Hill · The Daily Caller · Washington Examiner · Christian Science Monitor · NPR · Al Jazeera

Lone Holdout Juror in Lindsay Clancy Trial Retained Trump Lawyer, Ex-Husband to Appear on 60 Minutes

The lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy triple murder trial, Michael Desronvil, has retained attorney Edward Paltzik, who previously represented President Donald Trump in several high-profile lawsuits. Desronvil, who has remained largely silent since the mistrial, issued his first formal statement, rejecting claims he ignored the law. Clancy, who admitted to killing her children in January 2023, remains at a state hospital while prosecutors decide whether to retry her. Her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, is set to speak publicly about the case in an upcoming 60 Minutes interview, where he will discuss his grief and the conspiracy theories surrounding the case.

Patrick Clancy, who testified during the trial, has faced online accusations of involvement in the killings despite no evidence supporting such claims. His attorney, Howard Cooper, has criticized the "relentless, escalating and destructive defamation campaign" against Clancy and her family. The trial ended in a mistrial after a 11-1 deadlock, with Desronvil believing Clancy planned the killings. Clancy’s defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, a condition that can lead to severe mental health issues, including hallucinations and delusions.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that Paltzik represented Trump in lawsuits against The New York Times and CBS, resulting in settlements of $16 million and $15 million respectively. The Guardian and BBC do not mention these specific settlements, though they both note Paltzik’s involvement in the case. The New York Post and CBS News do not mention Paltzik’s past representation of Trump, instead focusing on Clancy’s legal team and the defamation claims against Patrick Clancy. The Guardian and BBC attribute the claim about the defamation campaign to Clancy’s attorney, Howard Cooper, while The Daily Wire and CBS News also attribute this to Cooper. The Daily Wire and BBC both mention Desronvil’s statement that he was “cut off” by other jurors, while The New York Post and CBS News do not include this detail.

Sources The Daily Wire · Newsweek · The Guardian · CBS News · New York Post · BBC

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Ed Sheeran Addresses Gaza Situation at Philadelphia Concert Amid Tour Controversy

Ed Sheeran opened his solo concert in Philadelphia on Saturday with comments about the situation in Gaza, calling it "catastrophic and unjustifiable." He said he wants his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics, but acknowledged the humanitarian issue. Sheeran addressed the controversy that unfolded after his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped from the tour after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage. The rapper had said "Free Palestine" during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey and performed a song critical of Israel's military actions in Gaza following the Oct. 7 Hamas-led attacks. The controversy led to the removal of Macklemore from the tour, with venues like Gillette Stadium refusing to host the show due to his comments. Sheeran denied being responsible for the decision, blaming the tour promoter and venue owners. His supporting acts, including Finneas and Lukas Graham, withdrew in solidarity with Macklemore, leaving Sheeran to perform solo. Pro-Palestinian demonstrators gathered outside the stadium, some expressing disappointment that Sheeran did not take a stronger stance.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire reports that celebrities have "memory-holed" the October 7 attacks and now prioritize the Palestinian cause, while BBC and CBS News focus on the specific controversy involving Ed Sheeran and Macklemore. The Daily Wire attributes the shift in celebrity focus to a desire for "publicity and praise" and frames the Palestinian cause as a new "cause célèbre" akin to past issues like climate change or Trump-Russia collusion. BBC and CBS News provide more specific details about the removal of Macklemore from the tour, citing Robert Kraft's involvement and the financial donations pledged by both Macklemore and Sheeran. Al Jazeera and NPR also mention the protests and the public reactions of fans, but do not elaborate on the broader celebrity culture critique present in The Daily Wire. The Daily Wire also mentions the Venice Film Festival and the film "NAZA" receiving a standing ovation, which other accounts do not include.

Sources The Daily Wire · BBC · NPR · Newsweek · Al Jazeera · CBS News

No source labeled left covered this story.

Ukraine launches over 1,000 drones at Russia, including hundreds targeting Moscow

Ukrainian forces launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia overnight, with hundreds directed at Moscow, according to officials. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described the attack as "unprecedented," claiming 450 drones were shot down en route to the capital. The strikes damaged a major oil refinery and a residential building, with two people killed. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the strikes, calling them a significant blow to Russia’s war economy. Separately, Russian authorities reported a drone attack on a civilian bus in the Kherson region, killing two people, including an election official.

In the Kyiv region, at least four people were killed in Russian attacks, including three children, according to Ukrainian officials. The attacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to escalate long-range strikes against each other, with both sides targeting energy infrastructure and logistics hubs to disrupt the other’s war effort.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and ABC News both report that a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man were killed in separate attacks, while NPR and Newsweek attribute the deaths to a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district and Sofyino, respectively. BBC and Newsweek mention a 44-year-old woman killed in Sofyino, while Al Jazeera and ABC News report the same incident. NPR states that two people were killed in the Moscow region, while BBC and Newsweek report one person killed in Sofyino and another in Orekhovo-Zuevo. ABC News and Al Jazeera mention a fire at a 21-storey building that evacuated 400 people, while BBC and Newsweek report a fire at a three-storey building and a warehouse, respectively. NPR and Newsweek report that 138 Russian drones were launched, while Al Jazeera and ABC News report 1,600 Ukrainian drones intercepted, with 450 heading for Moscow.

Sources Al Jazeera · NPR · Newsweek · BBC · The Guardian · ABC News

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signs executive order on AI safety and kill switch

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order Friday aimed at enhancing AI oversight and potentially requiring a "kill switch" for advanced AI systems. The order focuses on independent audits and kill switches, addressing the lack of federal action on AI regulation. Newsom criticized the Trump administration for its inaction, stating that the federal government has failed to protect Americans from AI risks. The order accelerates the implementation of two recently passed California laws that establish frameworks for independent AI safety assessments. Newsom also mentioned convening a panel of experts to explore the concept of a kill switch further. Other Democratic presidential contenders, including Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker and former Vice President Kamala Harris, have also expressed concerns about AI safety and called for regulatory measures. The order follows prior actions by Newsom to regulate AI and social media, including the signing of technology-related bills in September 2026.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that Newsom's executive order targets independent auditors and kill switches, and that it aligns with the positions of AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic. It also notes that former Vice President Harris and Illinois Gov. Pritzker have also called for AI safety measures. Fox Business highlights Newsom's criticism of Trump and mentions the blocking of a federal AI kill switch bill by Sen. Rand Paul. It also notes that Trump has opposed new AI regulations and that AI executives have called for federal limits. The New York Post emphasizes the involvement of experts like Fei-Fei Li and mentions the veto of Senate Bill 1047 in 2024, which sought to add safety and liability requirements to AI firms. It also references Jacob Coxon's warnings about AI's potential to wipe out civilization.

Sources Axios · Fox Business · New York Post

No source labeled left covered this story.

DOJ won't enforce handgun ban for 18- to 20-year-olds

The Justice Department announced it will not criminally enforce a 1968 federal law that prohibits licensed gun dealers from selling handguns to individuals aged 18 to 20. Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser stated the law violates the Second Amendment. The decision means federal prosecutors will not pursue criminal charges against dealers who sell handguns to law-abiding 18- to 20-year-olds. The law remains on the books but is not being enforced. The DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel concluded the restriction is unconstitutional, though it did not address whether agencies like the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) can continue administrative enforcement. The Supreme Court has not ruled on the constitutionality of the law, and federal appellate courts remain split on the issue.

Where the accounts differ

Axios and The Federalist both state the DOJ will not enforce the law, but Axios notes the opinion does not affect state laws, while The Federalist does not mention this. CBS News and New York Post both mention the DOJ will not appeal a court decision on silencers, which Axios and Straight Arrow News do not. Straight Arrow News and CBS News attribute the statement about 18-year-olds being "mature enough to be drafted, vote, serve as a juror, and be sentenced to death" to Assistant Attorney General Gaiser, while Axios and The Federalist do not. Axios and The Federalist both mention the 5th Circuit's 2012 ruling, while CBS News and New York Post do not. Straight Arrow News and CBS News attribute the claim that 18- to 20-year-olds are responsible for a disproportionate share of gun violence to GIFFORDS, while Axios and The Federalist do not.

Sources Axios · The Federalist · CBS News · New York Post · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: 37 people died in a Nigerian prison cell due to unsafe conditions, causing panic and health crises for survivors.

Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody

Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria died in custody, according to officials. The Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), a paramilitary group working with police, initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report shared with AFP suggested overcrowding and poor ventilation in the detention facility were responsible. The deaths sparked protests and a 24-hour curfew in Minna, the capital of Niger state.

Survivors described being locked in a cell with no ventilation, struggling to breathe, and appealing for help. A survivor, Dauda Shehu, told journalists at a hospital that detainees were "jam-packed" and "scampering for where to get fresh air." A video showed bodies of young men, many appearing to be teenagers, lying on the ground. Volunteers and veiled women identified the bodies, while voices shouted curses on those responsible. A survivor, who asked not to be named, said he survived because he was near the cell’s entrance where he could breathe better.

Protests broke out on Thursday evening in Minna, with some protesters armed with sticks, machetes, and traditional hunting rifles. Security forces used tear gas and live rounds to disperse the crowd. At least one body was found on the streets. The NSCDC said the detainees were held during raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area. The state governor, Umar Bago, stated many of the dead were children aged 14 to 18 who had been working in the mines instead of going to school.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the NSCDC initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak but later an intelligence report suggested overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible. The BBC states the NSCDC initially blamed a disease outbreak but later said the cause was yet to be established. The Guardian mentions that the state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children aged 14 to 18, while the BBC refers to the state governor as Mohammed Umaru Bago. The Guardian includes a survivor’s account of being near the cell’s entrance and surviving, while the BBC includes a relative’s account of his son surviving because he was near a small window. The Guardian also describes a video showing bodies of young men and volunteers identifying them, which the BBC does not mention.

Sources The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

Trump says US has ‘permanent control’ of Greenland security: Does it?

The U.S. and Denmark have reached a deal on Greenland's security, with President Donald Trump claiming the U.S. has "permanent control" over the territory's security and "all other needs." The agreement, expected to be signed at the U.S. UN General Assembly, grants the U.S. the right to build additional military sites on Greenland without approval from Denmark or Greenland. The deal also bars U.S. adversaries from establishing military bases or making "sensitive investments" in Greenland without U.S. approval. Denmark and Greenland have acknowledged the deal but have not provided specific details. Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen stated the agreement "recognises Greenland’s interests" and is "to the benefit of us all." Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called it "great for NATO and Europe" as it "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area."

The agreement, which Trump called an "Infinite Life" Agreement, would remain in force even if Greenland were to become an independent state. The U.S. Department of State official cited by the BBC said the deal prevents non-NATO states like China and Russia from establishing military presence or making investments in Greenland that could threaten the U.S. However, the official did not mention potential U.S. mining rights in Greenland, which has significant rare-earth mineral deposits. Some observers suggest this could be what Trump refers to by "sensitive investments."

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and the BBC both state that the deal does not give the U.S. ownership of Greenland, while Just The News and FOX News do not mention this clarification. The BBC and Al Jazeera note that the deal requires parliamentary ratification in Denmark and Greenland, whereas Just The News and FOX News do not specify this requirement. The BBC and Al Jazeera mention that the deal bars non-NATO states from making "sensitive investments" in Greenland, while Just The News and FOX News refer to this as restricting adversaries from making such investments. The Washington Examiner does not provide specific details about the agreement, while the New York Post mentions that the U.S. will "immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence" in Greenland.

Sources Al Jazeera · BBC · Washington Examiner · Just The News · FOX News · New York Post

Trump Threatens to Demolish Kennedy Center Over Naming Dispute

President Donald Trump has threatened to shut down or demolish the Kennedy Center unless his name is added to the building, following a federal court ruling that blocked his attempt to rename the facility. The center, a national arts complex and memorial to President John F. Kennedy, was closed to the public after its board, controlled by Trump appointees, voted to shut it down for renovations. Trump claimed the center is in financial trouble and that its closure is necessary to prevent its collapse. A federal judge ordered the administration to provide 30 days’ notice before making any major structural changes, including demolition.

The dispute began when Trump’s appointees sought to rename the center “The Trump-Kennedy Center” and add his name to its facade. A federal judge rejected the plan, stating only Congress can rename the facility. Trump responded by threatening to close the center unless his name is included, and he was photographed reviewing a poster that appeared to show a plan to demolish it. The administration has cited “severe structural deterioration” as a reason for the closure, though critics argue the takeover accelerated the center’s financial decline.

Where the accounts differ

Slate and ABC News both report that Trump threatened to close or demolish the Kennedy Center unless his name is added, and that the center was closed after a court blocked his renaming attempt. The Guardian and Mother Jones add that Trump claimed the center is in financial trouble and that a ceiling collapse during a storm was cited as a safety concern for the closure. The Federalist, however, focuses on the cultural and political significance of the center, criticizing its exclusivity and the motives of its defenders, without mentioning the financial or structural reasons for the closure. The Federalist also attributes the center’s value to its exclusive events and proximity to Georgetown, which other accounts do not mention.

Sources Slate · Mother Jones · The Federalist · The Guardian · NPR · ABC News

Tech power players land seat at table for high-stakes dinner with Trump, Xi

President Donald Trump is planning to hold a state dinner next week to mark a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping, and several tech industry leaders are expected to attend. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook are both reportedly planning to attend the state dinner. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is also expected to attend the event. The tech leaders' anticipated attendance at the Trump-Xi state dinner comes at a time of geopolitical tensions, including over the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and access to both models and the chips that power them. The U.S. and China are locked in a competition in which the two world powers are racing to develop more capable AI tools, which have been a source of tension between the countries. China's access to specialized chips that power advanced AI models has been restricted through the U.S. government's use of export controls on advanced semiconductors, like those made by Nvidia. Huang has been critical of those restrictions and said in May that China has "all the chips they need" despite the U.S. restrictions.

Where the accounts differ

Fox Business reports that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang warned that China has "all the chips they need" despite U.S. restrictions, while The Daily Wire and New York Post do not mention this specific claim by Huang. The Daily Caller reports that a senior U.S. official disputed claims that China threatened to cancel the Trump-Xi meeting over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Fox Business and The Daily Wire do not mention this dispute. The Daily Wire and New York Post list Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman as attending the state dinner, while Fox Business and ABC News do not mention Bezos or Musk in this context. The Daily Wire and New York Post describe the state dinner as the "hottest ticket in town," while Fox Business and ABC News do not use this phrase.

Sources Fox Business · The Daily Caller · Slate · The Daily Wire · New York Post · ABC News

Fox News Poll: 71% think Trump administration lacks plan to end Iran war

A new Fox News national survey indicates that a majority of voters believe the Trump administration lacks a clear strategy for ending the war with Iran. The poll found that 71% of voters think the administration lacks a plan to end the conflict. Additionally, 47% of voters say the war will make the U.S. less safe in the long run, up from 39% in April. The poll also shows that 60% of voters believe the decision to take military action against Iran was the wrong decision, compared to 37% who think it was right.

The survey highlights growing concerns about the war's impact on national security and public opinion. It notes that attitudes against the war have increased across most demographic groups, with the largest shifts among Hispanic voters, voters under age 30, moderates, and voters 65 and over. The poll also found that 32% of voters think the war will make the country safer, while 20% say there will be no difference.

Where the accounts differ

FOX News reports that 71% of voters think the Trump administration lacks a plan to end the Iran war, while the other outlets do not mention this specific poll or its findings. The Washington Examiner focuses on congressional concerns and the midterm elections, without addressing the Iran war or public opinion on it. CBS News, NPR, and Axios cover the immigration enforcement criticism by Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, but none mention the Fox News poll or the Iran war. The Daily Caller also covers Salazar’s ad but does not reference the Fox News survey or the Iran war.

Sources FOX News · Washington Examiner · CBS News · NPR · Axios · The Daily Caller

Lone Lindsay Clancy Holdout Juror Breaks His Silence

The lone male holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy’s triple-murder trial has spoken out, stating he had no doubts about her criminal responsibility. Michael P. Desronvil, 48, said he was cut off during deliberations when trying to explain different theories, and that the evidence presented by the prosecution was sufficient to prove Clancy knew exactly what she was doing. The jury deadlocked on whether Clancy was criminally responsible, leading to a mistrial declared by Judge William Sullivan on September 4. Clancy admitted to killing her three children but her defense argued she suffered from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors claimed she understood the nature of her actions.

The trial, which drew national attention, centered on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the deaths of her children. Jurors were split 11-1, with Desronvil the only one who believed she was guilty. His comments come after other jurors described the holdout as resistant to persuasion and accused him of refusing to listen to the mostly white women on the jury.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and Newsweek both report that Desronvil is a father from a Haitian immigrant family who moved to the United States in 1982. The New York Post does not mention his family background. The Daily Wire and FOX News both mention that Desronvil’s brother previously denied that religion played any role in his decision, while Newsweek does not. CBS News and BBC both report that Desronvil said he had no doubts, but the Daily Wire adds that he directly refuted claims he disregarded the law or lied under oath. The Daily Wire and BBC report that a juror named Roni described a moment when she believed the panel had reached a breakthrough, while CBS News and Newsweek do not mention this. The Daily Wire and FOX News both report that Desronvil’s lawyer, Edward Paltzik, described him as an “American Hero and Champion of Justice,” while the New York Post does not mention this.

Sources The Daily Wire · CBS News · Newsweek · FOX News · BBC · New York Post

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Russians head to the polls to choose lawmakers for their parliament

Russian voters are casting ballots in parliamentary elections from Friday to Sunday, marking the first such vote since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The elections are expected to be dominated by United Russia, the ruling party led by President Vladimir Putin, with little genuine opposition on the ballot. Yabloko, the only registered party openly opposing the war, was removed from the ballot by the Supreme Court on a technicality related to American copyright law. The election is seen as a means for the Kremlin to reinforce its control and legitimacy, with candidates largely avoiding discussion of the war or economic concerns.

The election environment is characterized by strict government control, with candidates avoiding sensitive topics and focusing on safe, non-controversial messages. Campaigns have been minimal, and televised debates have often been empty or scripted. The Kremlin is believed to be managing the election to ensure a predictable outcome, with little room for public dissent or alternative viewpoints.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Yabloko was banned from the ballot due to a technicality involving American copyright law, while Al Jazeera states the Supreme Court cited the party's antiwar stance as akin to seeking the violation of Russia’s territorial integrity. The Guardian and Newsweek both mention Yabloko's removal but do not specify the legal reasoning. The Christian Science Monitor and Al Jazeera note that the Kremlin is managing the election to suppress dissent, with the latter emphasizing the removal of managed opposition parties like Yabloko and the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF).

Sources NPR · The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Newsweek · Christian Science Monitor

No source labeled lean-right or right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Illegal foreign donations to Democratic fundraising platform ActBlue could undermine election integrity and democratic processes for millions of voters.

House GOP report details how Dem fundraising platform ActBlue allowed illegal foreign donations

A House Republican-led report released this week alleges that ActBlue, a Democratic fundraising platform, allowed illegal foreign donations to flow into U.S. campaigns with minimal verification. The report, obtained by the House Oversight, Judiciary, and Administration Committees, claims that ActBlue’s fraud safeguards, including passport verification, could be bypassed by foreign actors. Internal documents show that ActBlue’s system only checks for the number of characters in a passport number, without verifying its validity against a government database. The report also states that ActBlue instructed its fraud analysts to “give the donor the benefit of the doubt,” even when contributions originated from foreign IP addresses or had other red flags.

ActBlue’s CEO, Regina Wallace-Jones, refused to testify before the House Administration Committee, invoking her Fifth Amendment rights. The report claims that every member of ActBlue’s legal and compliance team left the platform after the 2024 election due to its “knowing and willful” acceptance of illegal foreign contributions. ActBlue has denied wrongdoing, calling the investigation a “political stunt” and accusing Republicans of attempting to silence organizations that threaten their agenda.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and The Federalist both report that ActBlue’s passport verification process only checks for the number of characters in a passport number, without verifying its validity. The Daily Caller adds that foreign donors could bypass the system by providing a random number with the correct number of digits. The Federalist also notes that ActBlue’s internal documents show supervisors instructed analysts to accept donations from donors with Hong Kong IP addresses and “a few foreign IPs” because they were “all consistently in the same place.” The New York Post and The Federalist do not mention this specific instruction. The Daily Caller also reports that ActBlue’s internal Slack messages show that the company retaliated against attorneys who raised concerns about lawbreaking, including deleting messages and terminating a law firm.

Sources New York Post · The Federalist · The Daily Caller

No source labeled center or lean-left or left covered this story.

The brief ends here.

The Fed raises interest rates. And, EU proposes Canada become an 'associate member'

The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to raise interest rates for the first time in more than three years, increasing the benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. The hike makes it more expensive to borrow money, grow a business or carry a credit card balance. Inflation has risen amid the war in Iran, driving up the price of gasoline and diesel fuel. While higher interest rates won't immediately lower prices, they demonstrate the Fed's commitment to restoring price stability, despite repeated pressure from President Trump to lower interest rates.

The European Union has proposed making Canada its first-ever "associate member." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the proposal for the new model of membership during her annual speech to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney emphasized how much the EU and Canada have in common and said that "Europe and Canada are stronger together." The EU says it wants to create a relationship with Canada unlike any it has built before.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that Trump's demands for lower rates came up frequently during Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference, while Axios and The Hill do not mention this. Fox Business and Al Jazeera report that Trump called Canada's potential EU associate membership "laughable" and warned of heavy tariffs, while NPR and Newsweek do not mention this. Newsweek states that Todd Belt, a professor at George Washington University, said Trump underestimated Carney's resolve, while other accounts do not mention this. Axios and The Hill report that Trump threatened to impose 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, while NPR and Fox Business do not mention the specific percentage.

Sources NPR · Axios · Newsweek · The Hill · Fox Business · Al Jazeera

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump withdraws Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, as his nominee to lead ICE

The White House withdrew its nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Thursday. Schroyer, who has little experience in immigration, was close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. The White House provided no explanation for the withdrawal. ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since the Obama administration, with David Venturella currently serving as acting director. Schroyer's nomination had stalled in the Senate Homeland Security Committee, where Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., had delayed the process until the White House provided more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis earlier this year.

Schroyer's nomination was announced by Trump in June, with the president calling him a "PATRIOT with real operational experience" and a "proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst." The withdrawal marks another setback for Trump's immigration agenda, which has faced criticism over its handling of enforcement operations and the deaths of civilians during raids. Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings.

Where the accounts differ

NPR and UPI both state that Schroyer had little experience in immigration and that his nomination had stalled in the Senate Homeland Security Committee. BBC and New York Post mention that Schroyer had no experience leading a law enforcement agency. Just The News and The Daily Wire do not mention Schroyer's experience in immigration or law enforcement leadership. The Daily Wire focuses on the hiring and vetting of ICE officers, which is not covered in the other accounts. UPI states that the Senate hasn't confirmed an ICE director since 2014, while NPR and BBC say since 2017. New York Post and UPI mention that the acting director can stay in place for up to 210 days unless another nominee is announced, which is not mentioned in the other accounts.

Sources NPR · BBC · Just The News · New York Post · The Daily Wire · UPI

U.S. Officials Held Secret Talks With Iran-Backed Houthis in Oman Amid Escalating Yemen Conflict

U.S. officials reportedly held undisclosed talks with Iran-backed Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend as the rebels made major battlefield gains against Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The meeting took place at the U.S. Embassy in Muscat and was facilitated by the Omani government, according to Reuters. The Houthis allegedly told American officials they had no intention of attacking U.S. vessels and remained committed to a 2025 ceasefire with Washington. A Yemeni source also said the Houthis pledged not to attack Israeli or other commercial vessels, except for Saudi ships. The State Department did not confirm the meeting but stated that protecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and preventing the export of terrorism from the Middle East remain core U.S. interests.

The conflict has intensified with Yemeni government forces reporting strikes on Houthi positions around Mocha and drone attacks in Marib. The Houthis claimed to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet over Marib. Saudi Arabia has requested missile defense support from allies as its stock of interceptors dwindles. U.S. officials have reiterated support for Yemen’s internationally recognized government, while the Houthis have seized control of key areas near the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical shipping route.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Caller and Al Jazeera both report that U.S. officials held direct talks with Houthi representatives in Oman, but only the Daily Caller and Al Jazeera mention that the Houthis allegedly told U.S. officials they had no intention of attacking U.S. vessels and remained committed to the 2025 ceasefire. The Daily Caller also notes that a Yemeni source said the Houthis pledged not to attack Israeli or other commercial vessels, except for Saudi ships, while Al Jazeera does not include this detail. The Newsweek article does not mention the U.S.-Houthi talks or the ceasefire commitment, instead focusing on the broader context of the conflict and historical parallels. The UPI and FOX News do not mention the U.S.-Houthi talks at all, with FOX News instead emphasizing the threat to Saudi oil production and the involvement of Iran. The NPR article does not mention the U.S.-Houthi talks but highlights the impact of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil exports and the humanitarian crisis in Yemen.

Sources The Daily Caller · Al Jazeera · Newsweek · UPI · FOX News · NPR

No source labeled lean-right or left covered this story.

Mike Johnson Cancels Thursday Votes, Sends House Home Early

Speaker Mike Johnson announced Wednesday that the House would send Congress home early for a seven-week recess ahead of the November midterms. The move comes as Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution and engaging in unlawful military actions. Massie argued that the early recess was a direct response to his impeachment resolution, which would have forced a vote within two legislative days. Johnson, however, dismissed the impeachment effort as a “publicity stunt” and claimed the early recess was to allow members to campaign for re-election.

Massie accused Johnson of using the calendar to avoid politically sensitive votes, including the impeachment of Hegseth and a discharge petition to force the release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein. He claimed the speaker could have held the impeachment vote earlier, calling the recess the “Hegseth holiday.” The Pentagon defended Hegseth, stating the “entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision.”

Where the accounts differ

Mother Jones and The Hill both report that Massie attributed the early recess to the impeachment resolution, though Mother Jones notes Johnson did not directly link the recess to the impeachment. The Hill adds that Massie claimed the resolution was privileged, forcing a vote within two days, which Johnson ignored by sending Congress home early. Axios and The Guardian both state Johnson called the impeachment a “publicity stunt,” while The Daily Wire and UPI include additional context about the Epstein discharge petition and the broader legislative agenda. The Guardian also notes Johnson’s claim that the House has been the second most productive in history, a point not mentioned in other accounts.

Sources Mother Jones · The Hill · Axios · UPI · The Daily Wire · The Guardian

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Trump Threatens to Demolish Kennedy Center Unless His Name Is Recognized

President Donald Trump has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center unless his administration receives recognition for its efforts to renovate the venue. A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to provide 30 days’ notice before any demolition or major structural changes to the center. The ruling follows a court battle over Trump’s attempts to rename the center after himself, which a judge previously blocked. The administration claims the center is in severe structural disrepair and needs urgent repairs, though critics argue the takeover has worsened its financial and reputational decline.

The Kennedy Center, established by Congress as a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy, has been under Trump’s control since the administration replaced its bipartisan board with loyalists. Trump has argued that the center is in “very, very bad shape” and that his involvement is necessary to secure funding for its $257 million renovation. The center temporarily closed earlier this week, with officials citing safety concerns after a ceiling collapse during a storm. However, critics, including Rep. Joyce Beatty, argue the closure may be a tactic to bypass court orders and proceed with renovations without oversight.

Where the accounts differ

Slate reports that Trump replaced the center’s bipartisan board with sycophants and that the new board named him chairman, while ABC News and The Guardian describe the board as being controlled by Trump appointees. Axios and BBC note that the board voted to close the center for renovations, but The Guardian adds that the closure was initially claimed to be temporary for safety reasons. The Dispatch does not mention the board’s composition or the closure, focusing instead on the structural condition of the building. BBC and The Guardian both mention a photo of Trump looking at a placard reading “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED,” while Slate and Axios describe a similar image but do not attribute it to a specific outlet.

Sources Slate · Axios · ABC News · BBC · The Guardian · The Dispatch

No source labeled right covered this story.

UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

The UN Human Rights Council's fact-finding mission concluded there were "reasonable grounds to believe" the US committed war crimes in two strikes on civilian targets in Iran. The first strike, on 28 February, hit a primary school in Minab, killing at least 156 people, including 120 children, according to local authorities. The second strike, also on 28 February, targeted a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd, killing at least 21 civilians, including seven children. The experts said both attacks were indiscriminate and constituted war crimes. The US military has not released findings of its own investigation into the Minab strike, though Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has stated the US would "never target civilian targets." The UN report also detailed Iran's violent crackdown on protests, including mass arrests, torture, and executions.

The UN mission found that the school in Minab was "clearly identifiable" and that no evidence indicated it was used for military purposes. The experts cited media reports suggesting a preliminary US military inquiry found US forces responsible, and the fact that the US is the only party to the conflict that possesses Tomahawk missiles. They concluded the school was the intended target and that the damage did not result from an errant strike or collateral damage. The US military disputes reports identifying the weapon used in the Lamerd strike as a Precision Strike Missile and claims it carried out no strikes there that day.

Where the accounts differ

BBC and The Guardian both state that the UN experts concluded the US committed war crimes in both strikes, citing the use of Tomahawk missiles and Precision Strike Missiles. UPI and Axios also report similar findings, though UPI mentions the school strike was due to outdated intelligence and President Trump claimed it was done by Iran. CBS News and New York Post focus more on the political response to the report, with the New York Post highlighting the White House's denial of the findings and the UPI reporting on congressional actions. The Guardian and BBC both mention the US military's failure to verify targeting data, while the New York Post attributes the school strike to outdated maps and Trump's claim of Iranian responsibility.

Sources BBC · New York Post · UPI · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

House votes to hold ex-Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt

The US House of Representatives voted to hold Leon Black in contempt of Congress on Wednesday after he ignored subpoenas for further testimony and information. The House passed the contempt resolution by unanimous consent following a bipartisan vote from the Oversight Committee. Black, a billionaire and former CEO of Apollo Global Management, had previously appeared for a voluntary interview with the committee in June but left before it ended. His attorneys claim he cooperated by providing a confidentiality agreement related to Epstein and that the committee is seeking information that does not exist.

Black’s legal team argued that the committee’s subpoenas were invalid and exceeded its authority, accusing Chairman James Comer of abusing power. They stated that Black provided the only confidentiality agreement Epstein knew about and that Ghislaine Maxwell had no involvement in any agreements. The Department of Justice will now decide whether to take action on the contempt resolution, though it is not required to do so.

Where the accounts differ

The New York Post and ABC News both state that Black paid Epstein $158 million between 2012 and 2017, while The Guardian and NPR report the amount as $170 million from 2013 to 2017. The Guardian and NPR also mention that Black described the payments as for tax and estate planning services, a detail not included in the New York Post or ABC News accounts. The BBC and Straight Arrow News report that Black paid Epstein $158 million, but the BBC adds that he described the payments as for legitimate reasons, a claim not made by other outlets. The Guardian and NPR note that Black’s attorneys claimed the committee is seeking information that does not exist, while the New York Post and ABC News attribute this claim to Black’s legal team without specifying the exact wording.

Sources New York Post · The Guardian · NPR · BBC · ABC News · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled lean-right covered this story.

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Over 300 women suffered unnecessary breast removals, leading to physical harm and long-term health complications.

Women told breasts removed needlessly as NHS trust finds more than 300 suffered harm

The County Durham and Darlington foundation trust (CDDFT) has informed the BBC that more than 300 women were harmed during breast cancer treatment at its unit. The trust is conducting an internal review of cases from January 2023 to February 2025, as well as 640 former patients who contacted a dedicated helpline. Of 514 cases reviewed so far, 315 patients have been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died. The trust has also identified cases where cancer diagnoses were missed or delayed, leading to cancer spread in some patients. Denise Howarth, a 51-year-old from Consett, was told her mastectomy could have been avoided. She had initially undergone a lumpectomy, then a mastectomy, along with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. She received the news in September 2025. Jo, a former NHS worker, was told in a phone call earlier this year that her mastectomy could have been avoided. She now feels "mutilated" and describes the mistakes as "absolutely unforgivable."

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that the trust is considering extending the review to cases dating back to 2015, which could involve up to 10,000 medical records. The Guardian does not mention this potential extension. The BBC also states that the National Crime Agency is working with Durham Police to investigate criminal offences, while the Guardian reports that the trust has been contacted for additional comment and does not specify the involvement of the National Crime Agency. The Guardian mentions that the trust has ended the outsourcing arrangement for breast cancer services, while the BBC notes that the trust has ended this arrangement but does not specify when.

Sources BBC · The Guardian

Trump Rips Fed Rate Hike But Gives Kevin Warsh A Pass

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years, increasing its target rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4.0%. President Donald Trump criticized the decision, calling for lower rates, but praised Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom he nominated earlier this year. Trump claimed he had advised Warsh to vote with the Fed board, as he believed the outcome would not change. Warsh stated that inflation remained elevated and that the rate hike would support a faster return to the Fed’s 2% inflation target.

Trump expressed confidence in Warsh despite the Fed’s decision, calling the board “hostile and political.” He also reiterated his belief that U.S. interest rates should be 1% or less. Meanwhile, Sen. Elizabeth Warren softened her tone toward Warsh, acknowledging his actions as a signal that he was “committed to bringing inflation under control,” though she stopped short of fully endorsing him.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and BBC both report that Trump called for lower interest rates and praised Warsh, but only the Daily Wire mentions Trump’s claim that he told Warsh to vote with the board. The BBC notes that Trump said the Fed board was “hostile,” a claim also made by The Daily Wire and ABC News. The Washington Examiner and Axios both mention Trump’s criticism of the Fed board, but only Axios includes Trump’s specific quote about the “hostile” board. The Hill and ABC News report that Trump accused the Fed of raising rates for political reasons, a claim not included in the Daily Wire or BBC accounts. The Daily Wire and BBC both attribute the statement about inflation being “too high and had been for too long” to Warsh, while The Hill and ABC News attribute it to Warsh as well. The Daily Wire and BBC both mention Trump’s social media post calling for lower rates, but only the Daily Wire includes the exact quote “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!” The Daily Wire and BBC both report that Trump said he was “aligned with Kevin,” but only the Daily Wire includes the specific quote about Warsh being “central casting.”

Sources The Daily Wire · BBC · Washington Examiner · Axios · The Hill · ABC News

Ed Sheeran Responds To The Macklemore Mess: ‘I Am Not Complicit’

Ed Sheeran stated he is not complicit in the removal of rapper Macklemore from his tour, asserting that the decision was made by the promoters, not himself. Sheeran said venues on his tour informed him they would pull their shows if Macklemore remained on the bill, following the rapper’s two controversial performances at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. Sheeran emphasized that he does not use his platform for politics, as his audience comes from diverse backgrounds and does not expect political opinions. He also noted that Macklemore’s contract for the tour was with the promoter, not him. Macklemore, in turn, blamed Robert Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots, for orchestrating his cancellation, claiming Kraft told Sheeran he would not be allowed to perform at Gillette Stadium, which Kraft owns. The tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, confirmed that multiple venues had said they would not allow a concert with Macklemore on the lineup.

Macklemore alleged that Kraft, whose company owns Gillette Stadium, refused to let him perform during Sheeran’s upcoming shows at the Massachusetts venue and “rallied” other stadium owners to take the same position. He claimed that Sheeran was in a difficult position and that refusing to take a side between the oppressor and the oppressed left him in a neutral stance. Macklemore also implied that Sheeran was a coward for not taking sides, suggesting that the stage had become a space for resistance.

Where the accounts differ

The Daily Wire and The Hill both state that Sheeran said venues told him they would pull their shows if Macklemore stayed on the bill, while The Nation and CBS News describe the decision as being made by the promoters. The Hill and The Nation mention that Sheeran asked Kraft to match a $2 million donation to Palestinian humanitarian aid, which is not mentioned in The Daily Wire or CBS News. The Nation and CBS News attribute the decision to Kraft’s influence, while The Daily Wire and The Hill state that the decision was made by the promoters. The Nation and CBS News also describe Kraft as a “friend of Donald Trump” and a “mega-donor to AIPAC,” which is not mentioned in The Daily Wire or The Hill.

Sources The Daily Wire · Mother Jones · The Hill · The Nation · NPR · CBS News

Congress passes sweeping US sanctions bill targeting Russia

The House of Representatives passed a bipartisan sanctions bill targeting Russia over its continued war in Ukraine, sending it to President Donald Trump’s desk. The legislation, named after late Senator Lindsey Graham, includes provisions for up to 100% tariffs on countries importing Russian energy and sanctions on Russian officials, banks, and a shadow fleet of tankers. The bill passed with a vote of 262 to 159, marking the first time in more than two years the US Congress has passed legislation supporting Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been a vocal advocate for the bill’s passage. While most Democrats supported the bill, some, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, opposed it due to concerns over the tariff authorities granted to Trump.

Where the accounts differ

Al Jazeera and The Hill both report that the bill passed with a 262-159 vote, but The Hill specifies that 203 Republicans, 58 Democrats, and one Independent voted in favor, while 7 Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed. Al Jazeera does not mention the breakdown of votes. The Hill and FOX News both note that 58 Democrats joined Republicans to pass the bill, while Al Jazeera and Axios do not specify the number of Democrats who supported the bill. The Hill and FOX News also mention that the bill includes a provision extending sanctions on Iran, which is not explicitly stated in Al Jazeera or Axios. The Hill and FOX News attribute the opposition of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries to concerns over Trump’s tariff authority, while Al Jazeera and Axios attribute his opposition to the bill’s loopholes and potential for exploitation.

Sources Al Jazeera · The Hill · Axios · Newsweek · FOX News · Washington Examiner

Lawmakers and leaders debate AI regulation amid growing concerns

Lawmakers across the U.S. are grappling with how to regulate artificial intelligence, with some expressing concern over its potential risks and others advocating for minimal government intervention. A growing number of politicians, including several senior lawmakers, have admitted they do not use AI personally, raising questions about their ability to craft effective policies. Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has dismissed warnings about AI as a "hoax," arguing that a strong president should be able to manage the technology without additional regulations. At the same time, figures like Rep. Chip Roy and Sen. Bernie Sanders have called for more oversight, emphasizing the need for a "human-first" approach to AI development. Industry leaders and some lawmakers have also raised alarms about the technology's potential to disrupt jobs, national security, and societal norms, prompting calls for a slowdown in its advancement.

The debate has intensified following recent warnings from AI executives and researchers, who have urged caution as the technology continues to evolve rapidly. Some lawmakers, like Rep. Frank Pallone and Sen. Mazie Hirono, have acknowledged their limited understanding of AI but argue that legislation is still necessary. Others, such as Sen. Tim Kaine, have stated they do not need to use AI personally to form opinions on its regulation. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has pushed for federal preemption of state-level AI regulations, a stance that has drawn criticism from lawmakers and advocacy groups.

Where the accounts differ

Axios reports that more than two dozen lawmakers said they don't use AI or have rarely done so, while BBC highlights Trump's dismissal of AI concerns as a "hoax" and his endorsement of the technology. The Daily Caller notes that Rep. Chip Roy broke with Trump on AI, calling for increased guardrails, while CBS News and The Guardian both mention Roy's skepticism of Trump's stance. NPR and CBS News describe bipartisan calls for a "human-centric" approach to AI, while The Guardian adds that Sanders and Bannon offered competing visions for dealing with China in the AI race. Axios and CBS News both mention Rep. Frank Pallone's statement about not needing to use AI to regulate it, but CBS News includes additional context about his spokesperson's comments.

Sources Axios · BBC · The Daily Caller · NPR · CBS News · The Guardian

EU's Ursula von der Leyen proposes Canada as first associate member

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the European Union's first associate member during her annual State of the Union address at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. She framed the move as part of a broader alliance aimed at creating "a common prosperity and economic security space." The proposal comes amid deteriorating U.S.-Canada relations, with President Donald Trump imposing tariffs and suggesting Canada could become the 51st state. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the proposal, calling for a "unique alliance" with the EU to reduce economic dependence on the U.S. Canada has already joined the EU's defense procurement program, and discussions are expected to continue at a Canada-EU summit in Montreal.

Von der Leyen described the expanded partnership as covering advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity, and economic security. She emphasized shared democratic values, stating that "democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work." Carney is set to address the European Parliament on Thursday, and the EU is seeking to deepen ties with Canada without granting full membership.

Where the accounts differ

NPR reports that von der Leyen proposed Canada as the first associate member and that Carney welcomed the idea, while Al Jazeera and Fox Business note Trump's criticism of the proposal, calling it a "hostile act" and warning of heavy tariffs. Axios and Newsweek describe Trump's reaction as dismissing the idea as "laughable" and threatening tariffs. The Guardian does not mention Trump's reaction but focuses on Carney's push for a "unique alliance" with the EU. NPR and Newsweek both mention that Canada has joined the EU's defense procurement program, while Al Jazeera and Fox Business do not. Axios and The Guardian note that associate membership is not yet defined under EU treaties, while NPR and Newsweek describe it as a new status.

Sources NPR · Al Jazeera · Axios · Fox Business · Newsweek · The Guardian

No source labeled right covered this story.

Trump says Kennedy Center to close as court rules his name must stay off building

The Kennedy Center board voted to close the performing arts center for two years, following a federal judge's ruling that blocked the addition of Trump's name to the building. The closure comes amid ongoing legal challenges to Trump's efforts to rebrand the institution. Trump claimed the closure was for safety reasons and that renovations cannot begin until the court rules on the board's approved name. He also vowed to take the case to the Supreme Court if the ruling is negative. The center's administration has stated it is on the brink of bankruptcy, with concerns about covering payroll obligations.

A federal judge, Christopher Cooper, ruled that the board cannot install memorials for Trump or anyone else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's approval. The judge cited a statute that established the center as a memorial to President John F. Kennedy. The board's proposal to add language to the center's name and campus was deemed to violate this statute and a previous court order. The center's closure is contingent on the judge lifting a temporary block that requires it to stay open while a lawsuit brought by board member Joyce Beatty proceeds.

Where the accounts differ

BBC reports that Trump claimed the board voted "almost unanimously" to close the venue "for safety reasons" and that the closure "will take place immediately." Washington Examiner states that Beatty said Trump "threw a tantrum" during a board meeting and claimed the venue is still open despite Trump's assertion. The Guardian and CBS News both mention that Trump and his allies on the board warned of financial and physical ruin for the center if no action is taken. Axios notes that the closure timing and duration were not confirmed, while Straight Arrow News reports that the board argued the center is in "dire" financial and structural shape.

Sources BBC · Washington Examiner · The Guardian · CBS News · Axios · Straight Arrow News

No source labeled right covered this story.

Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel

Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has placed a hold on a $2.8bn arms sale to Israel, citing concerns over the use of 2,000lb bombs in accordance with US law and protections for civilians. The sale includes 40,000 bombs, comprising 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s, and 20,000 I-2000 Penetrator warheads. Meeks emphasized that the decision does not reflect a lack of support for Israel’s defense needs but rather a responsibility to ensure weapons are used lawfully. The sale is part of a broader pattern of arms transfers to Israel since Trump took office, with over $12bn in weapons cleared or expedited.

The sale is subject to informal congressional review, where top lawmakers can delay the process before formal notification to Congress. While Meeks cannot unilaterally block the sale, his hold carries significant weight. The State Department has not yet commented on the matter, though the administration has previously bypassed congressional review in cases of national security emergencies.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian and Al Jazeera both report that the sale includes 40,000 bombs, with specific breakdowns of 20,000 MK-84s, 20,000 BLU-117s, and 20,000 I-2000 warheads. The Guardian adds that the sale is funded through US Foreign Military Financing. The Washington Examiner and Just The News also mention the same breakdown but do not specify the funding mechanism. The Daily Wire and BBC do not mention the funding method. The Guardian and BBC note that the sale is part of a broader pattern of arms transfers to Israel since Trump took office, while the Daily Wire provides additional context on the rationale for the sale, including the use of heavy bombs in underground warfare.

Sources The Guardian · Al Jazeera · Washington Examiner · BBC · Just The News · The Daily Wire

Below the fold — the model's one nomination, reason printed: Climate change-linked Nepal-Tibet floods displaced thousands, destroying homes and livelihoods while worsening global climate crisis impacts.

Climate change played role in Nepal-Tibet flood, study finds

A study has found that climate change likely contributed to the avalanche of rock and ice that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border. The disaster, which killed over 1,300 people and left more than 5,000 missing, was caused by a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres falling from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August. The collapse sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres of snow and ice into the valley below, triggering flash floods that swept away homes, roads, bridges and other infrastructure. The event registered as an earthquake and moved at speeds exceeding 110 mph.

The World Weather Attribution study, led by Dr Friederike Otto of Imperial College London, identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, with temperatures in July and August 2026 being around 1.5C warmer than the 30-year average. The study also noted that the freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost. The researchers concluded that climate change was a destabilising factor on a pre-existing geological predisposition, but not the sole cause of the disaster.

Where the accounts differ

The Guardian reports that the death toll is around 1,300 with more than 5,000 people missing, while the BBC states the death toll remains at around 1,400, with the number of missing revised to 6,150. The Guardian attributes the glacier collapse to a combination of factors including climate breakdown, glacier recession, and the 2015 earthquake, but does not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause. The BBC states that the study found climate change was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition," but not the only cause. The Guardian mentions that the study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause, while the BBC does not mention this nuance.

Sources The Guardian · BBC

No source labeled lean-left or lean-right or right covered this story.

The brief ends here.
